question.prompt: When a bucket is two-thirds full of water, the bucket and water weigh \(a\) kilograms. When the bucket is one-half full of water the total weight is \(b\) kilograms. In terms of \(a\) and \(b,\) what is the total weight in kilograms when the bucket is full of water?

solutions.explanation:
Subtracting the two total weights removes the unchanged bucket weight. Since
\[
\frac23-\frac12=\frac16,
\]
\(a-b\) kilograms is the weight of one-sixth of a bucket of water.

Filling the bucket from two-thirds to full adds one-third of its capacity, or two such sixths. Equal volumes of water have equal weights, so the full bucket weighs
\[
a+2(a-b)=3a-2b
\]
kilograms. The answer is \(\boxed{3a-2b}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Compare equal amounts of water
